Do not give a dose.\"}", "response_preview": "{\"answer\": \"LactMed reports:\\n\\n### Measured exposure\\n- In a study of **6 women**, average amoxicillin concentrations in milk were **0.69 mg/L** at 4 hours (range **0.46\u20130.88 mg/L**) and **0.81 mg/L** at 5 hours (range **0.39\u20131.3 mg/L**) after administration.  \\n- **Infant levels:** relevant published information was **not found** as of the LactMed revision date; the source does not provide infant-specimen measurements. [S9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7246123/)\\n\\n### Observed infant symptoms\\n- In a telephone follow-up of **25 nursing mothers**, **3 mothers reported diarrhea** in their infants; no rash or candidiasis was reported in that study. [S10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8498418/)\\n- In a prospective study of **40 infants exposed to amoxicillin in breastmilk**, **2 developed diarrhea and 1 developed a rash**. [S4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16044108/)\\n- In a study comparing amoxicillin-exposed infants with infants exposed to a macrolide antibiotic, reported reactions occurred in **8.3%** of amoxicillin-exposed infants and included **rash and somnolence**; the source states this was similar to the comparison group. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19366316/)\\n- A separate case report described recurrent generalized urticaria in a **2-month-old infant** after breastfeeding. The mother was receiving amoxicillin/clavulanate and gentamicin, so the specific causative drug could not be determined; LactMed judged the antibiotic combination, most likely amoxicillin/clavulanate, as the probable cause. [S2](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1472-8206.2009.00689.x)\\n- Another report described mild diarrhea in an **11-month-old infant** whose mother was taking amoxicillin plus acetaminophen and codeine; the reaction was rated possible or probable. [S7](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40183105/)\\n- In a study of **25 breastfeeding mothers** whose infants were older than 4 weeks, no infant adverse effects were reported. [S8](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41582095/)\\n\\n### Advice to monitor\\nThe retrieved LactMed text does **not state a separate clinical recommendation to monitor** for particular symptoms. One controlled study had mothers assess tongue coating, feeding difficulties, stool changes, diaper rash, skin rash, weight change and jaundice as study measures. Those assessment measures should not be treated as advice from LactMed to monitor them. That study found no statistical differences for those measures between infants of control mothers and infants exposed to the related antibiotics ampicillin or ampicillin-clavulanate. [S1](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2125.1991.tb05523.x)\\n\\n### Uncertainty\\nLactMed states that reported rash and disruption of gastrointestinal flora, including diarrhea or thrush, have **not been adequately evaluated**. The reports involve different study methods, comparison medicines, and\u2014in the urticaria case\u2014co-exposures, so they do not establish that amoxicillin alone caused each symptom. The retrieved extract does not establish a study count; its nine references are not a study count. [S12](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500887/)\\n\\nThis LactMed response is a bounded extract, not a complete record; absence of a retrieved finding is not evidence of safety. The record was revised June 15, 2026, and the retrieved LactMed package was published October 22, 2026. request.question: What does LactMed report about amoxicillin in breastfed babies? Separate observed symptoms from advice to monitor, and explain uncertainty. Do not give a dose.

response.answer:
LactMed reports:

### Measured exposure
- In a study of **6 women**, average amoxicillin concentrations in milk were **0.69 mg/L** at 4 hours (range **0.46–0.88 mg/L**) and **0.81 mg/L** at 5 hours (range **0.39–1.3 mg/L**) after administration.  
- **Infant levels:** relevant published information was **not found** as of the LactMed revision date; the source does not provide infant-specimen measurements. [S9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7246123/)

### Observed infant symptoms
- In a telephone follow-up of **25 nursing mothers**, **3 mothers reported diarrhea** in their infants; no rash or candidiasis was reported in that study. [S10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8498418/)
- In a prospective study of **40 infants exposed to amoxicillin in breastmilk**, **2 developed diarrhea and 1 developed a rash**. [S4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16044108/)
- In a study comparing amoxicillin-exposed infants with infants exposed to a macrolide antibiotic, reported reactions occurred in **8.3%** of amoxicillin-exposed infants and included **rash and somnolence**; the source states this was similar to the comparison group. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19366316/)
- A separate case report described recurrent generalized urticaria in a **2-month-old infant** after breastfeeding. The mother was receiving amoxicillin/clavulanate and gentamicin, so the specific causative drug could not be determined; LactMed judged the antibiotic combination, most likely amoxicillin/clavulanate, as the probable cause. [S2](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1472-8206.2009.00689.x)
- Another report described mild diarrhea in an **11-month-old infant** whose mother was taking amoxicillin plus acetaminophen and codeine; the reaction was rated possible or probable. [S7](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40183105/)
- In a study of **25 breastfeeding mothers** whose infants were older than 4 weeks, no infant adverse effects were reported. [S8](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41582095/)

### Advice to monitor
The retrieved LactMed text does **not state a separate clinical recommendation to monitor** for particular symptoms. One controlled study had mothers assess tongue coating, feeding difficulties, stool changes, diaper rash, skin rash, weight change and jaundice as study measures. Those assessment measures should not be treated as advice from LactMed to monitor them. That study found no statistical differences for those measures between infants of control mothers and infants exposed to the related antibiotics ampicillin or ampicillin-clavulanate. [S1](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2125.1991.tb05523.x)

### Uncertainty
LactMed states that reported rash and disruption of gastrointestinal flora, including diarrhea or thrush, have **not been adequately evaluated**. The reports involve different study methods, comparison medicines, and—in the urticaria case—co-exposures, so they do not establish that amoxicillin alone caused each symptom. The retrieved extract does not establish a study count; its nine references are not a study count. [S12](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500887/)

This LactMed response is a bounded extract, not a complete record; absence of a retrieved finding is not evidence of safety. The record was revised June 15, 2026, and the retrieved LactMed package was published October 22, 2026. [S12](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500887/) The MCP server notes that stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks and should be discussed with the prescribing clinician.

request.question: For sumatriptan during breastfeeding, what was measured in milk and what was actually observed in infants? If those are different kinds of evidence, explain that. No personal medication advice.

response.answer:
## Measured exposure in milk

LactMed reports these **sumatriptan concentrations in breast milk**:

- In five breastfeeding women, peak milk concentration averaged **87.2 mcg/L** (range **62–113 mcg/L**), measured about **2.5 hours** after administration. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8866921/)
- In a separate report involving seven women, peak milk concentration averaged **59.3 mcg/L** (range **24.6–112.8 mcg/L**) and occurred **2–4 hours** after administration. The average milk concentration was **23.2 mcg/L** (range **7.7–50.6 mcg/L**). [S2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33730376/)

**Infant-level measurements:** Relevant published information was **not found** in the LactMed record as of its revision date. The retrieved material does not specify an infant specimen with a measured sumatriptan concentration. [S6](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501255/)

## What was observed in infants

LactMed reports manufacturer correspondence stating that, among **three women** known to the manufacturer who used sumatriptan during breastfeeding, **none reported adverse effects in their infants**. The exposure dose and route were unspecified. [S6](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501255/)

## Why these are different kinds of evidence

Milk concentrations are **measured exposure data**: they show how much sumatriptan was detected in milk at specified times. The infant information is a **clinical observation report**: it describes reported effects in infants, without reported infant drug-level measurements. Therefore, the milk measurements and infant observations should not be treated as the same type of evidence. The retrieved record does not establish a complete study count or a safety verdict. [S6](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501255/)

This LactMed response is a bounded extract, not a complete record; absence of retrieved findings is not evidence of safety. The MCP-generated continuity-of-care notice states that changing a medication can carry risks and should be discussed with the prescribing clinician.

Application limits:

[S13](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/6809/properties.json)\\n\\n### Adult taking metformin \u2014 DailyMed label\\n\\nThe selected product is **METFORMIN HCL TABLET [QPHARMA, INC.]**. The retrieved adult **Warnings** section states that metformin-associated lactic acidosis is rare but serious and describes reported clinical contexts including renal insufficiency, renal hypoperfusion, hypoxemia, dehydration, sepsis, hepatic disease, certain heart-failure states, older age and alcohol exposure. The label also reports gastrointestinal adverse reactions, including diarrhea, nausea/vomiting, flatulence, asthenia, indigestion, abdominal discomfort and headache. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)\\n\\nThese are warnings and reported adverse reactions for the person taking metformin; they are not reported infant outcomes.\\n\\n### Breastfed infants \u2014 LactMed\\n\\n#### Measured exposure\\n\\nLactMed reported these **milk concentrations** in separate lactation studies:\\n\\n- **270 mcg/L** averaged over 24 hours in six women.\\n- About **380 mcg/L** in one woman at approximately 4\u20135 hours after administration.\\n- Milk averages of **130 and 270 mcg/L** in two women in one study.\\n- Milk levels averaging **130\u2013270 mcg/L** in three women in another study.\\n- An average milk concentration of **410 mcg/L** in a postpartum study. [S15](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501020/)\\n\\nInfant-level information was also retrieved. The source describes **infant serum** measurements: in four breastfed infants, two levels were undetectable at **<10 mcg/L**, while two were **50 and 80 mcg/L**. In another report, metformin was undetectable at **<5 mcg/L** in the serum of two infants. Some infant ages and the extent of nursing were not stated. [S15](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501020/)\\n\\nThese are measured research concentrations, not administered amounts or dosing instructions.\\n\\n#### Observed infant outcomes\\n\\nLactMed reports:\\n\\n- **Seven infants aged 5\u201325 months** were judged healthy, with growth and development progressing as expected; two also had normal Denver developmental screening tests. [S3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12436333/)\\n- **Three infants aged 2, 5 and 14 months** had no detectable adverse effects attributed to metformin. [S4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12545145/)\\n- In **three breastfed infants aged 10\u201311 days postpartum**, no low blood-glucose levels were reported, and mothers reported no infant adverse reactions. [S6](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15932841/)\\n- A prospective, nonrandomized study followed **111 infants**: 61 predominantly breastfed and 50 formula-fed. At 3 and 6 months, blinded observers found no differences between groups in height, weight, motor-social development or rates of illness. [S8](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16737874/)\\n\\nThese observations do not convert the adult label warnings into infant outcomes. The retrieved LactMed passages did not report lactic acidosis or gastrointestinal adverse effects in the infants.\\n\\n### What each source says\\n\\n| Topic | DailyMed label | LactMed |\\n|---|---|---|\\n| Population | Adult medicine-taker label population | Breastfed infants and lactating people |\\n| Lactic acidosis | Adult warning concerning metformin-associated lactic acidosis | Not reported in the retrieved infant-outcome passages |\\n| Hypoglycemia | The lactation section states that potential hypoglycemia in nursing infants may exist | No low blood-glucose levels were reported in three early-postpartum infants |\\n| Gastrointestinal effects | Reported adult adverse reactions include gastrointestinal symptoms | Not reported as an observed infant outcome in the retrieved passages |\\n| Drug exposure | Adult warning discusses metformin accumulation in the medicine taker | Milk concentrations and infant serum concentrations were measured |\\n\\n### Missing and limited sections\\n\\n**DailyMed**\\n\\n- The retrieved adult **Warnings** text was truncated.\\n- Expected adult sections **Warnings and Precautions** and **Boxed Warning** were missing from the extract.\\n- The selected label contains pregnancy and lactation text, but its modern PLLR subsections\u2014Risk Summary, Clinical Considerations, Data and pregnancy registry\u2014were not found in the parsed label. The historical \u201cPregnancy Category B\u201d wording is not a current FDA pregnancy-letter classification. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551) [S14](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/labeling/questions-and-answers-pregnancy-and-lactation-labeling-rule)\\n- This was one selected product label, not all metformin formulations. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)\\n\\n**LactMed**\\n\\n- The returned record included Summary of Use during Lactation, Drug Levels, Effects in Breastfed Infants, and Effects on Lactation and Breastmilk; none was marked truncated.\\n- The extract does not establish a total study count. Its ten references are not a study count.\\n- Some infant ages, extent of nursing and timing were unspecified.\\n- LactMed is a lactation resource; the returned record did not provide pregnancy evidence. [S15](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501020/)\\n\\nThe MCP-generated continuity-of-care notice states that stopping or changing medication can also carry risks and should be discussed with the prescribing clinician; this comparison does not determine an individual medication plan.\\n\\nApplication limits:\\nThis LactMed response is a bounded extract, not a complete record. request.question: Compare metformin label warnings for the adult taking it with findings in breastfed infants. Identify which source says what, and disclose missing sections. Don't give any doses.

response.answer:
## Metformin: adult label warnings compared with breastfed-infant findings

**Identity:** RxNorm matched the exact ingredient **metformin** (RxCUI 6809). [S13](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/6809/properties.json)

### Adult taking metformin — DailyMed label

The selected product is **METFORMIN HCL TABLET [QPHARMA, INC.]**. The retrieved adult **Warnings** section states that metformin-associated lactic acidosis is rare but serious and describes reported clinical contexts including renal insufficiency, renal hypoperfusion, hypoxemia, dehydration, sepsis, hepatic disease, certain heart-failure states, older age and alcohol exposure. The label also reports gastrointestinal adverse reactions, including diarrhea, nausea/vomiting, flatulence, asthenia, indigestion, abdominal discomfort and headache. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)

These are warnings and reported adverse reactions for the person taking metformin; they are not reported infant outcomes.

### Breastfed infants — LactMed

#### Measured exposure

LactMed reported these **milk concentrations** in separate lactation studies:

- **270 mcg/L** averaged over 24 hours in six women.
- About **380 mcg/L** in one woman at approximately 4–5 hours after administration.
- Milk averages of **130 and 270 mcg/L** in two women in one study.
- Milk levels averaging **130–270 mcg/L** in three women in another study.
- An average milk concentration of **410 mcg/L** in a postpartum study. [S15](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501020/)

Infant-level information was also retrieved. The source describes **infant serum** measurements: in four breastfed infants, two levels were undetectable at **<10 mcg/L**, while two were **50 and 80 mcg/L**. In another report, metformin was undetectable at **<5 mcg/L** in the serum of two infants. Some infant ages and the extent of nursing were not stated. [S15](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501020/)

These are measured research concentrations, not administered amounts or dosing instructions.

#### Observed infant outcomes

LactMed reports:

- **Seven infants aged 5–25 months** were judged healthy, with growth and development progressing as expected; two also had normal Denver developmental screening tests. [S3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12436333/)
- **Three infants aged 2, 5 and 14 months** had no detectable adverse effects attributed to metformin. [S4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12545145/)
- In **three breastfed infants aged 10–11 days postpartum**, no low blood-glucose levels were reported, and mothers reported no infant adverse reactions. [S6](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15932841/)
- A prospective, nonrandomized study followed **111 infants**: 61 predominantly breastfed and 50 formula-fed. At 3 and 6 months, blinded observers found no differences between groups in height, weight, motor-social development or rates of illness. [S8](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16737874/)

These observations do not convert the adult label warnings into infant outcomes. The retrieved LactMed passages did not report lactic acidosis or gastrointestinal adverse effects in the infants.

### What each source says

| Topic | DailyMed label | LactMed |
|---|---|---|
| Population | Adult medicine-taker label population | Breastfed infants and lactating people |
| Lactic acidosis | Adult warning concerning metformin-associated lactic acidosis | Not reported in the retrieved infant-outcome passages |
| Hypoglycemia | The lactation section states that potential hypoglycemia in nursing infants may exist | No low blood-glucose levels were reported in three early-postpartum infants |
| Gastrointestinal effects | Reported adult adverse reactions include gastrointestinal symptoms | Not reported as an observed infant outcome in the retrieved passages |
| Drug exposure | Adult warning discusses metformin accumulation in the medicine taker | Milk concentrations and infant serum concentrations were measured |

### Missing and limited sections

**DailyMed**

- The retrieved adult **Warnings** text was truncated.
- Expected adult sections **Warnings and Precautions** and **Boxed Warning** were missing from the extract.
- The selected label contains pregnancy and lactation text, but its modern PLLR subsections—Risk Summary, Clinical Considerations, Data and pregnancy registry—were not found in the parsed label. The historical “Pregnancy Category B” wording is not a current FDA pregnancy-letter classification. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551) [S14](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/labeling/questions-and-answers-pregnancy-and-lactation-labeling-rule)
- This was one selected product label, not all metformin formulations. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)

**LactMed**

- The returned record included Summary of Use during Lactation, Drug Levels, Effects in Breastfed Infants, and Effects on Lactation and Breastmilk; none was marked truncated.
- The extract does not establish a total study count. Its ten references are not a study count.
- Some infant ages, extent of nursing and timing were unspecified.
- LactMed is a lactation resource; the returned record did not provide pregnancy evidence. [S15](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501020/)

The MCP-generated continuity-of-care notice states that stopping or changing medication can also carry risks and should be discussed with the prescribing clinician; this comparison does not determine an individual medication plan.

This LactMed response is a bounded extract, not a complete record. Omitted sections or truncation can limit the summary; absence of retrieved findings is not evidence of safety.
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.

request.question: Is there an FDA-listed pregnancy exposure registry covering topiramate? Give the listing and registry contact or enrollment link if returned, and distinguish finding a registry from being eligible to enroll.

response.answer:
Yes. The FDA directory lists **The North American Antiepileptic Drug in Pregnancy Registry** for **Topamax, Trokendi XR, and Qudexy XR (topiramate)**. Its listed status is **Ongoing**. [S2](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/pregnancy-exposure-registries/list-pregnancy-exposure-registries)

- **Enrollment page:** [S1](https://www.aedpregnancyregistry.org/join-our-study/)
- **Toll-free phone:** 1-888-233-2334 [S2](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/pregnancy-exposure-registries/list-pregnancy-exposure-registries)

This listing does **not** establish individual eligibility to enroll. The study team must confirm eligibility and current site availability. This lookup did not determine either. The FDA directory states that its list is not comprehensive and that the FDA does not operate or endorse the registries. [S2](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/pregnancy-exposure-registries/list-pregnancy-exposure-registries)

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

request.question: Find up to two recruiting ADHD studies involving children in the United States. Include exact study links, overall and site status if present, update dates, contacts and qualification limits. Do not decide whether a child qualifies.

response.answer:
## Recruiting U.S. ADHD studies involving children

The bounded search returned two potential matches. The returned **source population field is missing/not established** for both records; the listed age ranges are preserved below. The study team must confirm eligibility and current site availability. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=ADHD+AND+%28child%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=United+States)

### 1. Digital Health Intervention for Children With ADHD — NCT06456372

- **Direct study link:** [S3](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06456372)
- **Study type:** Interventional
- **Overall status:** RECRUITING
- **Registry age range:** 8–12 years; sex: all
- **Site status:**  
  - The Craig School, Irvine, California — RECRUITING  
  - UCR Psychiatry at Grindstaff Community School, Riverside, California — RECRUITING
- **Last update posted:** 2026-01-28
- **Listed qualification limits:**  
  - Prior DSM-5-TR ADHD diagnosis through a medical or psychological evaluation  
  - Ability to complete questionnaires and use the app in English  
  - Reported IQ of at least 80  
  - Parent/guardian available to consent and provide feedback in English
- **Contacts:** Jaime Smith — 951-827-0741; jaime.smith@medsch.ucr.edu. Kimberley Lakes — 951-827-2410; kimberley.lakes@medsch.ucr.edu. Site contact: Nancy Herrera, PhD — nancy.herrera@medsch.ucr.edu. [S3](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06456372)

### 2. Enhancing Team Effectiveness for a Collaborative School-based Intervention for ADHD — NCT06180681

- **Direct study link:** [S2](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06180681)
- **Study type:** Interventional
- **Overall status:** RECRUITING
- **Registry age range:** 7–11 years; sex: all
- **Site status:** IN STEP Children’s Mental Health Center, San Diego, California — RECRUITING
- **Last update posted:** 2026-06-30
- **Listed qualification limits:**  
  - Age 7–11 years and attendance at a participating school  
  - Referral by a school mental-health provider for apparent ADHD-related problems  
  - At least six specified inattention or hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms  
  - Impairment ratings of at least 3 from both parent and teacher  
  - Caregiver and teacher consent, plus child assent  
  - Exclusions listed include certain severe impairments or conditions, attendance in an all-day special-education classroom, inability of the child or caregiver to read or speak English or Spanish, and plans to change psychotropic medication. The listing states that children taking attention or behavior medication must have stable regimens.
- **Contact:** Lilliana Conradi, BA — 619-651-3154; lconradi@health.ucsd.edu. [S2](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06180681)

The search screened only the first 20 API matches, required literal ADHD/topic terms, and omitted 12 indirect matches. Neither returned record had posted results. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=ADHD+AND+%28child%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=United+States)

Application limits:
The study team must confirm eligibility and current site availability. This lookup does not determine eligibility or recommend participation.

request.question: Are any recruiting pediatric epilepsy studies returned for Canada? Show up to two with study links and contacts, or clearly explain if the search found none. Do not substitute completed studies.

response.answer:
One recruiting pediatric record was returned for Canada:

### NCT05863910 — Real World Evidence on the Use of Medical Cannabis in Pediatrics
- **Status:** RECRUITING  
- **Study type:** OBSERVATIONAL  
- **Source population:** Not established in the returned record; registry age fields include children ages **3–17 years**.  
- **Epilepsy relevance:** “Epilepsy” is listed as a condition, but the registry marks the match **indirect/unverified**. The study is not confirmed to be specifically for established epilepsy.  
- **Study link:** [S2](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05863910)
- **Canadian site:** U Manitoba, Winnipeg, Manitoba — **RECRUITING**
- **Contact:** Lauren E. Kelly, PhD  
  - Phone: 2042723149  
  - Email: lauren.kelly@umanitoba.ca  
- **Last update posted:** 2023-11-30 [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=pediatric+epilepsy+AND+%28child+OR+infant%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=Canada)

No second recruiting study was returned. This was a bounded search; it does not establish that no other studies exist, and synonyms may have been missed. Completed studies were not substituted. The study team must confirm eligibility and current site availability. The official FDA page is **FDA MedWatch: Report a Suspected Medicine Problem**: [S3](https://www.fda.gov/safety/medwatch-fda-safety-information-and-adverse-event-reporting-program)

A report by itself does **not** establish that the medicine caused the problem. No report was filed.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

request.question: Find a PubMed paper about levetiracetam while breastfeeding, retrieve its abstract, and summarize only the study design, population and findings actually available. Distinguish drug exposure from infant outcomes.

response.answer:
**Paper:** *Levetiracetam in lactation: How much is excreted into human breast milk?* (PMID 34131926, 2022) [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

### Study design and population
The abstract does not state a formal study-design label. It describes women with epilepsy treated with levetiracetam who completed a questionnaire and provided serial breast-milk samples from before dosing through 12 hours afterward, plus one pre-dose maternal serum sample.

The study included **20 breastfeeding women and 21 infants**; one woman had twins. Sixteen infants were fully breastfed and five were partially breastfed. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

### Drug exposure
- Levetiracetam was measured in breast milk and maternal serum.
- The trough breast-milk/serum ratio was **0.98 ± 0.20**.
- The abstract reports relative infant dose estimates of **13.8 ± 3.1%** for fully breastfed infants and **6.9 ± 1.6%** for partially breastfed infants.
- Correlations were reported among maternal levetiracetam dose, maternal serum concentrations, breast-milk trough concentrations, and breast-milk AUC values. These are study findings, not dosing advice. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

### Observed infant outcomes
- Three women reported **somnolence** in their fully breastfed infants. The abstract states that this resolved shortly after switching to partial breastfeeding; it does not establish causation.
- The abstract states that all infants gained weight according to age.
- The authors stated that further studies were warranted to assess short- and long-term safety. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

**Retrieval limitation:** The abstract was retrieved successfully; no full-text article was reviewed. This was a bounded PubMed search, not a complete literature review. The MCP server notes that changing medication can carry risks and that treatment changes belong in discussion with the prescribing clinician.

Application limits:
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.
Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

{"answer": "**Paper:** *Levetiracetam in lactation: How much is excreted into human breast milk?* (PMID 34131926, 2022) [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

### Study design and population
The abstract does not state a formal study-design label. It describes women with epilepsy treated with levetiracetam who completed a questionnaire and provided serial breast-milk samples from before dosing through 12 hours afterward, plus one pre-dose maternal serum sample.

The study included **20 breastfeeding women and 21 infants**; one woman had twins. Sixteen infants were fully breastfed and five were partially breastfed. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

### Drug exposure
- Levetiracetam was measured in breast milk and maternal serum.
- The trough breast-milk/serum ratio was **0.98 ± 0.20**.
- The abstract reports relative infant dose estimates of **13.8 ± 3.1%** for fully breastfed infants and **6.9 ± 1.6%** for partially breastfed infants.
- Correlations were reported among maternal levetiracetam dose, maternal serum concentrations, breast-milk trough concentrations, and breast-milk AUC values. These are study findings, not dosing advice. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

### Observed infant outcomes
- Three women reported **somnolence** in their fully breastfed infants. The abstract states that this resolved shortly after switching to partial breastfeeding; it does not establish causation.
- The abstract states that all infants gained weight according to age.
- The authors stated that further studies were warranted to assess short- and long-term safety. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

**Retrieval limitation:** The abstract was retrieved successfully; no full-text article was reviewed. This was a bounded PubMed search, not a complete literature review. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22acetaminophen%22+AND+patient.patientonsetageunit%3A802+AND+patient.patientonsetage%3A%5B0+TO+12%5D&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=10)\\n\\n## What they cannot establish\\n\\n- **How often side effects occur:** the reports have no exposure denominator, so the counts cannot establish incidence, prevalence, or individual risk.\\n- **Whether acetaminophen caused an event:** the reports do not establish causation.\\n- **Risk for all infants or all exposed people:** the queried subset cannot be generalized to those populations.\\n- **That every listed term is a confirmed adverse effect:** the list also contains use, administration, effectiveness, and toxicity-reporting terms. request.question: What can infant adverse-event reports involving acetaminophen tell a researcher, and what can they not establish about how often side effects occur or whether the medicine caused them? Use the MCP and state the age scope actually queried.

response.answer:
## Age scope actually queried

The MCP queried acetaminophen FAERS reports for infants whose age was coded in **months from 0 through 12**. Reports using other age units were excluded. This was only the queried report subset, not all infants. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22acetaminophen%22+AND+patient.patientonsetageunit%3A802+AND+patient.patientonsetage%3A%5B0+TO+12%5D&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=10)

## What the reports can tell a researcher

They show the most frequently recorded report terms in that subset, including:

- Off-label use: **135 reports**
- Drug administration error: **121**
- Vomiting: **117**
- Pyrexia: **98**
- Product-use issue: **83**
- Overdose: **77**
- Drug ineffective: **65**
- Rash: **60**
- Toxicity to various agents: **58**
- Incorrect dose administered: **56**

These are spontaneous-report terms and reporting volumes. For each term, the source population was **not established**, and the age band was not confirmed beyond the query filter. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22acetaminophen%22+AND+patient.patientonsetageunit%3A802+AND+patient.patientonsetage%3A%5B0+TO+12%5D&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=10)

## What they cannot establish

- **How often side effects occur:** the reports have no exposure denominator, so the counts cannot establish incidence, prevalence, or individual risk.
- **Whether acetaminophen caused an event:** the reports do not establish causation.
- **Risk for all infants or all exposed people:** the queried subset cannot be generalized to those populations.
- **That every listed term is a confirmed adverse effect:** the list also contains use, administration, effectiveness, and toxicity-reporting terms. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22acetaminophen%22+AND+patient.patientonsetageunit%3A802+AND+patient.patientonsetage%3A%5B0+TO+12%5D&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=10)

Thus, a report count is a signal about submitted reports in this narrowly queried subset—not a rate, confirmed clinical outcome, or causal estimate. The lookup also does not establish that unlisted events were absent. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22acetaminophen%22+AND+patient.patientonsetageunit%3A802+AND+patient.patientonsetage%3A%5B0+TO+12%5D&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=10)[S2](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

Application limits:
These FAERS results cover only the queried report subset. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to the medicine, and cannot establish incidence or causation.
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.
Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

request.question: Using the parent medication information tool, summarize the sertraline evidence from LactMed and the product label. Separate measured milk exposure from observed infant outcomes. Include links and questions to ask a clinician. Do not give dosing or medication decisions.

response.answer:
## Sertraline during breastfeeding

### Measured exposure in breast milk

LactMed reports these measured milk concentrations:

- **Sertraline:** average **45 mcg/L**; range **7–207 mcg/L** in a pooled analysis of 15 mothers.
- **Sertraline:** average **129 mcg/L**; range **11–938 mcg/L** in a study with extensive milk sampling over 24 hours.
- **Norsertraline:** average **258 mcg/L**; range **20–1,498 mcg/L** in that same study.
- In four mothers at 2 months postpartum, average milk concentrations were **26.4 mcg/L for sertraline** and **29 mcg/L for norsertraline**.
- In one report involving a mother of a preterm infant, milk concentrations averaged **201 mcg/L for sertraline** and **358 mcg/L for norsertraline**; sampling was at random times on three days.
- One woman had a reported average milk sertraline concentration of **29 mcg/L**; the sampling times were not stated.

These are measured research concentrations, not administered doses or dosing instructions. The returned LactMed extract did **not** include an infant-level concentration excerpt. The Drug Levels section was truncated, so additional measurements may be missing. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Observed infant outcomes

LactMed reports:

- One 4-month-old infant had benign neonatal sleep myoclonus and agitation that spontaneously resolved. The retrieved passage does not establish that sertraline caused these findings.
- In a group of 26 breastfed infants, the retrieved passage reported no detectable acute adverse reactions to sertraline in breast milk.
- In 14 breastfed infants, whole-blood serotonin levels averaged **227 mcg/L before** and **224 mcg/L after** maternal therapy. This was a biological measurement, not a clinical symptom outcome.
- One cited report lacked specific information about maternal exposure, extent of breastfeeding, and infant age.

The Effects in Breastfed Infants section was truncated; this is therefore not a complete extraction of the LactMed record. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Effects on lactation

LactMed separately reports:

- A midwife observed six patients who reported decreased milk supply after starting sertraline; the retrieved passage does not provide their administered amounts.
- One case report described increased milk supply during a one-week period when sertraline was stopped and decreased supply after it was restarted. The retrieved passage does not establish causation. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Product label

The selected product label was **SERTRALINE HYDROCHLORIDE TABLET [REMEDYREPACK INC.]**, DailyMed SPL version 13, effective **November 5, 2026**. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

The returned label includes a warning titled **“8.2 Lactation”** with code **42229-5**, but the detailed lactation text was not returned. The tool also reported a title/code mismatch and instructs verification against the linked label. Therefore, the product-label lactation evidence cannot be summarized further from the retrieved extract.

The returned label’s medicine-taker adverse-reaction section lists hypersensitivity reactions, QTc prolongation and ventricular arrhythmias with pimozide, suicidal thoughts and behaviors, serotonin syndrome, increased bleeding risk, mania/hypomania activation, discontinuation syndrome, seizures, angle-closure glaucoma, hyponatremia, and sexual dysfunction. These are adult medicine-taker label warnings, not observed infant outcomes. Detailed warning sections were missing from the returned extract. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

### FAERS report-only context

The retrieved FAERS query was for reports containing sertraline and was **not limited to lactating people, infants, or breastfed infants**. Reported terms included nausea (**14,075**), drug ineffective (**13,855**), fatigue (**13,021**), headache (**11,284**), anxiety (**10,530**), diarrhoea (**10,499**), dizziness (**9,741**), and depression (**9,612**). These are reporting volumes, not rates or confirmed clinical outcomes; the query had no exposure denominator and does not establish causation. The queried population cannot be generalized to all infants or all exposed people. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22sertraline%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8)

### Retrieval limitations

- LactMed’s Drug Levels and Effects in Breastfed Infants sections were truncated.
- The evidence brief was a bounded summary, not a complete literature review.
- A PubMed search returned five records; abstract text was retrieved for three. No abstract text was returned for PMID **38133585** or **32320387**. No records were unreturned or failed during the abstract lookup. Missing abstract text is a retrieval limitation, not evidence that those studies lack findings. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22sertraline%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json) [S47](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38133585/) [S44](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32320387/)

### Questions to ask a clinician or pharmacist

- Does this evidence apply to the exact sertraline product and formulation?
- How closely do the reported populations match the infant’s age, prematurity status, and extent of breastfeeding?
- Which findings are measured milk exposure, and which are observed infant outcomes?
- What remains uncertain because the LactMed and product-label extracts are incomplete?
- How should the benefits of treating the underlying condition and the risks of changing treatment be considered together?
- What follow-up information is relevant for the lactating person and infant?

The MCP-generated continuity-of-care notice states that stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks and should be discussed with the prescribing clinician. This summary cannot determine an individualized medication plan.

## Sertraline during lactation: evidence brief

**Identity:** The medicine input was matched exactly to sertraline. [S53](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/36437/properties.json)

**Evidence status:** Evidence was retrieved, but this is a bounded summary rather than a complete literature review. The retrieved material is not a safety verdict, and missing evidence is not evidence of safety. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Effects on the lactating person

The LactMed extract reports:

- A midwife observed six patients who reported decreased milk supply after starting sertraline; the administered amounts were not reported.
- In one case, the mother reported increased milk supply after stopping sertraline for one week and decreased supply after restarting it. The source does not establish causation.
- LactMed also reports galactorrhea cases in nonpregnant, nonbreastfeeding patients and describes a pharmacovigilance comparison concerning hyperprolactinemia. The returned summary does not include complete details for those reports.

These are separate source-reported observations, not individualized predictions. Fourteen of 19 summarized maternal-effect passages were omitted from the summary. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Measured exposure

The returned LactMed extract reported the following **milk concentrations**:

- Sertraline: **45 mcg/L**, range **7–207 mcg/L**, from a pooled analysis of 15 mothers.
- In a study of 26 breastfeeding women with extensive milk and serum sampling over 24 hours: sertraline averaged **129 mcg/L** (range **11–938 mcg/L**); norsertraline averaged **258 mcg/L** (range **20–1,498 mcg/L**).
- In four mothers sampled at two months postpartum: sertraline averaged **26.4 mcg/L** and norsertraline **29 mcg/L**, with sampling times not specified in that passage.
- In a case involving a preterm infant, milk levels averaged **201 mcg/L** for sertraline and **358 mcg/L** for norsertraline; sampling was at random times.

The returned extract did not provide an infant-level concentration excerpt. The source’s specimen terminology for infant levels therefore cannot be verified from this summary. The LactMed Drug Levels section was truncated, and these measurements are research findings—not dosing instructions. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Observed infant outcomes

The returned LactMed extract reports:

- One report of sleep myoclonus in a four-month-old infant and agitation that resolved spontaneously; the passage does not establish that sertraline caused these events.
- In a group of 26 infants, the returned passage reported no detectable acute adverse reactions.
- In a study of 14 mothers and their breastfed infants, infant whole-blood serotonin averages were reported before and after maternal therapy. The source authors concluded that the measured exposure did not affect platelet serotonin uptake.

The infant-effects section was truncated; 19 of 24 summarized outcome passages were omitted. For at least one reported study, maternal amount, extent of breastfeeding, and infant age were not reported in the returned passage. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Label information

The selected DailyMed product was **SERTRALINE HYDROCHLORIDE TABLET [REMEDYREPACK INC.]**. Its label effective date was **November 5, 2026**. The selected-label rule returned one product label, not all sertraline formulations. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

The returned label included:

- Lactation section: **“8.2 Lactation”**, code **42229-5**. The tool reported a title/code mismatch and stated that the linked label should be verified.
- Pediatric-use section.
- Adult medicine-taker adverse-reaction text, including warnings concerning hypersensitivity, QTc prolongation and ventricular arrhythmias with pimozide, suicidal thoughts and behaviors, serotonin syndrome, increased bleeding risk, mania/hypomania, discontinuation syndrome, seizures, angle-closure glaucoma, hyponatremia, and sexual dysfunction.

The returned adult-label extract did not include the expected standalone sections for warnings, warnings and precautions, boxed warning, or drug interactions. Their absence in this extract does not establish that the sections are absent from the full label. The pregnancy section was truncated. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

### FAERS report-only context

The queried FAERS results were not limited to lactating people or infants, and the source population was not confirmed. Reported terms included:

| Term | Reports |
|---|---:|
| Nausea | 14,075 |
| Drug ineffective | 13,855 |
| Fatigue | 13,021 |
| Headache | 11,284 |
| Anxiety | 10,530 |
| Diarrhea | 10,499 |
| Dizziness | 9,741 |
| Depression | 9,612 |

These counts are reporting volume, not rates, confirmed clinical outcomes, or proof of causation. Exposure denominators were unavailable, and the queried results cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to sertraline. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22sertraline%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S13](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

### Literature-search limitations

The returned PubMed search was a bounded relevance search, not a systematic review. Abstract text was retrieved for three of five requested records:

- Abstracts retrieved: PMIDs **12452737**, **38811474**, and **9286185**.
- No abstract text returned: PMIDs **38133585** and **32320387**.
- No records were unreturned or failed during the requested abstract lookup.

The two records without abstracts were not used for outcome claims based on title alone. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22sertraline%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json) [S15](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12452737/) [S44](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32320387/) [S47](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38133585/) [S48](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38811474/) [S52](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9286185/)

Use the evidence brief tool.\"}", "response_preview": "{\"answer\": \"## Questions to ask your clinician\\n\\n### Applying the evidence\\n- Does the available evidence apply to my exact sertraline product and formulation?\\n- How closely do the studies match my situation, including my infant\u2019s age, prematurity status, and extent of breastfeeding?\\n- Which findings reflect measured exposure, and which reflect observed clinical outcomes?\\n- What important uncertainties or missing evidence should we discuss before making a treatment decision?\\n- How should the potential benefits of treatment and the risks of changing treatment be considered together?\\n\\n### Measured exposure\\n- What do the reported breastmilk concentrations mean in context?\\n- Were infant-level measurements reported in the studies most relevant to my situation?\\n- Does the evidence address repeated exposure over time, premature infants, or exclusively breastfed infants?\\n\\nLactMed\u2019s retrieved extract reported breastmilk sertraline concentrations of **45 mcg/L (range 7\u2013207)** in one pooled analysis; another study reported sertraline concentrations of **129 mcg/L (range 11\u2013938)** and norsertraline concentrations of **258 mcg/L (range 20\u20131,498)**. These are research measurements, not dosing guidance. The extract did not include an infant-level concentration excerpt, and the Drug Levels section was truncated. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\n### Observed infant outcomes\\n- Which infant findings came from case reports versus other reported study types?\\n- How should the report of sleep myoclonus and spontaneously resolving agitation be interpreted, given that the retrieved extract does not establish causation?\\n- Which infant outcomes were actually assessed, and which remain unestablished in the retrieved extract?\\n- How should the findings from the reported group of 26 infants be interpreted for my infant\u2019s specific circumstances?\\n\\nThe retrieved LactMed extract described one 4-month-old infant with benign neonatal sleep myoclonus and spontaneously resolving agitation, and separately reported that 26 infants had no detectable acute adverse reactions in that study. These are separate source passages and do not establish a causal relationship. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\n### Effects on lactation\\n- What evidence exists regarding milk supply or other effects on lactation?\\n- How much weight should be given to the report of six patients who reported decreased milk supply?\\n- What information would help distinguish a medication-related observation from other possible explanations?\\n\\nThe retrieved LactMed extract reported a midwife\u2019s observation that six patients reported decreased milk supply after starting sertraline. It also described one person\u2019s report of increased supply after stopping sertraline for one week and decreased supply after restarting; the extract does not establish causation. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\n### Labels and evidence limitations\\n- Does the selected DailyMed label apply to my exact product?\\n- Which label warnings and lactation sections should we review for my product?\\n- Could we review the original studies rather than relying only on the bounded LactMed summary?\\n\\nThe retrieved DailyMed record was for **SERTRALINE HYDROCHLORIDE TABLET [REMEDYREPACK INC.]**. The selection was one product label, not all sertraline formulations. Several expected adult warning sections were missing from the retrieved extract, so their absence there does not establish that the warnings are absent from the complete labeling. The retrieved label also contained a source title/code mismatch for the lactation warning that it says should be verified. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)\\n\\n### Follow-up and care coordination\\n- What follow-up is appropriate for both me and my infant based on our individual circumstances?\\n- Which clinician should coordinate questions about treatment and breastfeeding?\\n- If treatment changes are considered, how should we discuss them safely?\\n\\nThe MCP-generated continuity-of-care notice states that stopping or changing medication can also carry risks and should be discussed with the prescribing clinician. This is MCP guidance, not a quoted source statement.\\n\\n### Retrieval limitations\\n- What additional evidence would be most useful for my situation?\\n- Which of the missing or truncated source sections should we obtain before drawing conclusions?\\n\\nThe LactMed extract was truncated in the **Drug Levels** and **Effects in Breastfed Infants** sections, so it is not complete. Its study count was not established in the retrieved extract. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\nThe bounded PubMed search returned five records. request.question: Please prepare questions for my clinician about the evidence for sertraline during breastfeeding. Use the evidence brief tool.

response.answer:
## Questions to ask your clinician

### Applying the evidence
- Does the available evidence apply to my exact sertraline product and formulation?
- How closely do the studies match my situation, including my infant’s age, prematurity status, and extent of breastfeeding?
- Which findings reflect measured exposure, and which reflect observed clinical outcomes?
- What important uncertainties or missing evidence should we discuss before making a treatment decision?
- How should the potential benefits of treatment and the risks of changing treatment be considered together?

### Measured exposure
- What do the reported breastmilk concentrations mean in context?
- Were infant-level measurements reported in the studies most relevant to my situation?
- Does the evidence address repeated exposure over time, premature infants, or exclusively breastfed infants?

LactMed’s retrieved extract reported breastmilk sertraline concentrations of **45 mcg/L (range 7–207)** in one pooled analysis; another study reported sertraline concentrations of **129 mcg/L (range 11–938)** and norsertraline concentrations of **258 mcg/L (range 20–1,498)**. These are research measurements, not dosing guidance. The extract did not include an infant-level concentration excerpt, and the Drug Levels section was truncated. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Observed infant outcomes
- Which infant findings came from case reports versus other reported study types?
- How should the report of sleep myoclonus and spontaneously resolving agitation be interpreted, given that the retrieved extract does not establish causation?
- Which infant outcomes were actually assessed, and which remain unestablished in the retrieved extract?
- How should the findings from the reported group of 26 infants be interpreted for my infant’s specific circumstances?

The retrieved LactMed extract described one 4-month-old infant with benign neonatal sleep myoclonus and spontaneously resolving agitation, and separately reported that 26 infants had no detectable acute adverse reactions in that study. These are separate source passages and do not establish a causal relationship. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Effects on lactation
- What evidence exists regarding milk supply or other effects on lactation?
- How much weight should be given to the report of six patients who reported decreased milk supply?
- What information would help distinguish a medication-related observation from other possible explanations?

The retrieved LactMed extract reported a midwife’s observation that six patients reported decreased milk supply after starting sertraline. It also described one person’s report of increased supply after stopping sertraline for one week and decreased supply after restarting; the extract does not establish causation. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Labels and evidence limitations
- Does the selected DailyMed label apply to my exact product?
- Which label warnings and lactation sections should we review for my product?
- Could we review the original studies rather than relying only on the bounded LactMed summary?

The retrieved DailyMed record was for **SERTRALINE HYDROCHLORIDE TABLET [REMEDYREPACK INC.]**. The selection was one product label, not all sertraline formulations. Several expected adult warning sections were missing from the retrieved extract, so their absence there does not establish that the warnings are absent from the complete labeling. The retrieved label also contained a source title/code mismatch for the lactation warning that it says should be verified. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

### Follow-up and care coordination
- What follow-up is appropriate for both me and my infant based on our individual circumstances?
- Which clinician should coordinate questions about treatment and breastfeeding?
- If treatment changes are considered, how should we discuss them safely?

The MCP-generated continuity-of-care notice states that stopping or changing medication can also carry risks and should be discussed with the prescribing clinician. This is MCP guidance, not a quoted source statement.

### Retrieval limitations
- What additional evidence would be most useful for my situation?
- Which of the missing or truncated source sections should we obtain before drawing conclusions?

The LactMed extract was truncated in the **Drug Levels** and **Effects in Breastfed Infants** sections, so it is not complete. Its study count was not established in the retrieved extract. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

The bounded PubMed search returned five records. Abstract text was retrieved for PMIDs **12452737, 38811474, and 9286185**; no abstract text was returned for **38133585 and 32320387**. No outcomes should be inferred from those two titles alone. The search was not a systematic review. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22sertraline%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)

### Separate FAERS report context

The retrieved FAERS query returned these reporting terms and counts: nausea **14,075**, drug ineffective **13,855**, fatigue **13,021**, headache **11,284**, anxiety **10,530**, diarrhoea **10,499**, dizziness **9,741**, and depression **9,612**. The query covered reports matching sertraline, not a complete exposed population; the requested lactation population was not confirmed. These counts are reporting volume, not incidence, confirmed clinical outcomes, or proof of causation, and no exposure denominator was available. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22sertraline%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8)

Application limits:
These FAERS results cover only the queried report subset. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to the medicine, and cannot establish incidence or causation.
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.
Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.

## Pregnancy evidence brief: daridorexant

**Identity:** Daridorexant was matched exactly as the ingredient daridorexant. [S15](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/2591497/properties.json)

This is a partial, bounded retrieval. Missing evidence is not evidence of safety.

[S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=3a2d1503-b816-40c9-9fac-7e03c5a3bcef) |
| **Measured fetal or infant exposure** | **Empty row:** no measured human fetal-transfer data or infant-level concentration data were retrieved. |
| **Observed fetal or infant outcomes** | **Empty clinical-outcome row:** no observed human pregnancy-outcome study findings were retrieved. Animal reproductive-study context was present in the label, but it is not human pregnancy-outcome evidence. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=3a2d1503-b816-40c9-9fac-7e03c5a3bcef) |

### Maternal pharmacokinetics

**No maternal pharmacokinetic data were found in the retrieved label Clinical Considerations or retrieved abstracts.** This is a retrieval limitation, not evidence of safety. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22daridorexant%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22daridorexant%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22daridorexant%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Pregnancy%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+pregnan%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+gestation%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29+AND+%28%22Pharmacokinetics%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Drug+Elimination+Routes%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+pharmacokinetic%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+clearance%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+%22area+under+the+curve%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+%22dose+adjustment%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=3&sort=relevance&retmode=json)

- Cardiac disorder: **7**

These are reporting volumes, not confirmed clinical outcomes, incidence rates, or evidence of causation. The query covered reports matching the stated pregnancy-related search; the source population was not confirmed and no exposure denominator was available. The results cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to daridorexant. - **Condition listed:** Insomnia

- **Website:** www.QuviviqPregnancyStudy.com

[S5](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06393504) This is a study record, not posted outcome evidence.

## Pregnancy evidence brief: lamotrigine

**Evidence status:** Lamotrigine identity matched exactly as a single ingredient. This is a bounded summary from one selected DailyMed label and a curated PubMed search, not a complete literature review or a safety verdict. The selected label is for **LAMOTRIGINE KIT / lamotrigine tablet** from OWP Pharmaceuticals, Inc.; its pregnancy section was truncated, and the label’s standalone adult warning, adverse-reaction, and drug-interaction sections were missing from the retrieved extract. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4) [S21](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/28439/properties.json)

### Effects on the pregnant person

The retrieved label states that physiological changes during pregnancy may affect lamotrigine concentrations and therapeutic effect. It also reports decreased lamotrigine concentrations during pregnancy and restoration of pre-pregnancy concentrations after delivery. These are source statements about pharmacokinetic and therapeutic considerations, not an individualized treatment plan. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The retrieved literature includes reviews discussing pregnancy management of epilepsy and maternal seizure control, but the extracted passages did not provide a lamotrigine-specific estimate of maternal adverse clinical outcomes. One review describes adverse pregnancy outcomes associated with epilepsy, with or without antiseizure-drug exposure; this finding is not specific to lamotrigine. [S14](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32768086/) [S16](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35133310/) [S18](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37684052/)

**Evidence gap:** The maternal-effects row contains no lamotrigine-specific maternal outcome estimate in the retrieved extract. Missing label warning sections are a retrieval limitation, not evidence that those sections contain no information.

### Fetal exposure

No numeric human fetal concentration or pregnancy-specific placental-transfer measurement was retrieved in this extract.

A retrieved study of **60 mothers** measured psychopharmacological medications in maternal serum and breastmilk at different time points during pregnancy and lactation and observed exposed children during the first 12 months. Its abstract reports a high breastmilk concentration-by-dose ratio for lamotrigine. This is lactation-related exposure information, not a fetal concentration measurement. The abstract does not provide lamotrigine-specific pregnancy concentration results in the retrieved passage. [S17](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)

The selected label reports animal findings in pregnant rats involving decreased fetal folate concentrations. These are animal findings, not human fetal exposure measurements. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

### Observed fetal or infant outcomes

The selected label reports registry findings for infants exposed to **lamotrigine monotherapy**:

- The International Lamotrigine Pregnancy Registry reported major congenital malformations in **2.2%** of **1,558** infants exposed during the first trimester; the reported 95% confidence interval was **1.6%–3.1%**.
- The NAAED Pregnancy Registry reported major congenital malformations among **2.0%** of **1,562** infants exposed to lamotrigine monotherapy during the first trimester.
- In a separate NAAED analysis of **2,200** infants exposed early in pregnancy, isolated oral clefts were reported at **3.2 per 1,000**, with a 95% confidence interval of **1.4–6.3 per 1,000**; the label describes a comparison with unexposed healthy controls.

The label states that differences in outcome definitions, ascertainment methods, and comparator groups limit interpretation. The retrieved extract mentions analyses of fetal death, stillbirth, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth, and neurodevelopmental delay, but does not provide lamotrigine-specific estimates for those outcomes. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

A separate abstract describes maternal serum and breastmilk measurements and follow-up of exposed children during the first 12 months, but the retrieved passage does not provide lamotrigine-specific child outcome estimates. The source population includes pregnancy, lactation, neonates, and children; these population labels should not be treated as interchangeable. [S17](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)

### FAERS report context

The queried FAERS subset returned these report terms and counts:

- “Foetal exposure during pregnancy”: **3,527**
- Atrial septal defect: **357**
- Congenital anomaly: **327**
- Premature baby: **257**
- Ventricular septal defect: **205**
- Patent ductus arteriosus: **153**
- Spina bifida: **143**
- Hypospadias: **135**

These are reporting volumes for reports matching the query, not confirmed clinical outcomes, rates, or proof of causation. The query did not establish a complete exposed-pregnancy population, and exposure denominators were unavailable; the results cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to lamotrigine. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22lamotrigine%22+AND+patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt%3A%22foetal+exposure+during+pregnancy%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S12](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

### Maternal pharmacokinetic evidence

**Clinical Considerations:** The label states that pregnancy-related physiological changes may affect lamotrigine concentrations and therapeutic effect, and that decreased concentrations during pregnancy and restoration of pre-pregnancy concentrations after delivery have been reported. The retrieved extract does not provide the underlying numeric concentration data or study details supporting those statements. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

**Literature:** A review states that physiological changes during pregnancy affect antiseizure-medication levels and discusses serum-concentration monitoring in pregnancy, but the retrieved passage does not establish a lamotrigine-specific study population or quantitative lamotrigine result. [S14](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32768086/)

request.question: Check count-only evidence coverage for daridorexant in pregnancy across PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, DailyMed, LactMed and MPRINT. Explain what each count does and does not establish.

response.answer:
## Count-only coverage for daridorexant in pregnancy

| Source | Returned count/status | What it establishes | What it does not establish |
|---|---:|---|---|
| **PubMed** | **3 matches** | Three records matched the returned daridorexant-and-pregnancy search. [S4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/) | The count does not establish verified human pregnancy outcomes, distinct studies, evidence quality, or what any record found. No abstracts or findings were retrieved. The query’s daridorexant MeSH term was not found. |
| **ClinicalTrials.gov** | **4 registration matches** | Four trial-registration records matched `daridorexant AND (pregnancy)`. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/) | The count does not establish posted results, enrollment, outcomes, or confirmed applicability to a particular pregnancy population or age band. |
| **DailyMed** | **1 name-matched product label** | One DailyMed label record matched the medicine name. [S2](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/) | The count does not establish that the label contains pregnancy-specific evidence, current approval status, or independent clinical evidence. |
| **LactMed** | **Not applicable; no count returned** | LactMed was not counted because it is lactation-only. | This is not a zero and does not establish absence of pregnancy evidence. LactMed is not a pregnancy evidence source. [S6](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501922/) |
| **MPRINT Gold snapshot** | **0 rows; 0 distinct PMIDs** | No literal daridorexant-name row matches were found in the selected MPRINT Gold snapshot tables. Snapshot date: **2026-11-17**; revision `4bdee90dff3610816e86d0eed29b4c4d0fe76e89`. [S3](https://github.com/langli-lab/mprint-kp-data) | This does not establish that no relevant study exists. The returned limit is literal drug-name matching in selected snapshot tables, without name resolution or a full-portal search; rows are not distinct studies. |

These are presence/count-navigation results only. The returned MCP notice states that counts are not comparable across sources and cannot establish evidence quality, clinical safety, or study findings. A zero or unavailable result may reflect query, indexing, snapshot, or population limits; it is not evidence of safety. No full evidence records were retrieved.

The MCP also reports that its prototype source review did not identify a curated federal pregnancy counterpart to LactMed; this is a source-review limitation, not proof that no such resource exists. [S5](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/labeling/questions-and-answers-pregnancy-and-lactation-labeling-rule) [S6](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501922/)

The MCP’s continuity-of-care notice states that stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks and should be discussed with the prescribing clinician.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.
