No treatment decisions.\"}", "response_preview": "{\"answer\": \"## Sertraline during lactation\\n\\nSertraline was matched exactly as the single ingredient sertraline, RxNorm ID 36437. [S53](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/36437/properties.json)\\n\\n### Effects reported in the lactating person\\n\\nLactMed reports:\\n\\n- A midwife observed **6 patients who reported decreased milk supply after starting sertraline**; administered amounts were not reported.\\n- In one of those reports, the mother had taken sertraline since the sixth month of pregnancy, reported increased milk supply during a one-week interruption at four months postpartum, and reported decreased supply after restarting. The source does not establish the exact elapsed time between restarting and the reported decrease.\\n- LactMed also describes galactorrhea reports in nonpregnant, nonbreastfeeding patients and cites a French pharmacovigilance study in which sertraline was not found to have an increased risk of hyperprolactinemia compared with other drugs.\\n\\nThese are source-reported observations from a limited extract; the retrieved material does not establish a definitive study count. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\n### Measured exposure in milk\\n\\nThe retrieved LactMed record reported the following **milk concentrations**:\\n\\n- In a pooled analysis of 15 mothers: sertraline averaged **45 mcg/L**, range **7\u2013207 mcg/L**.\\n- In a study of 26 women with extensive milk and serum sampling over 24 hours: sertraline averaged **129 mcg/L**, range **11\u2013938 mcg/L**; norsertraline averaged **258 mcg/L**, range **20\u20131498 mcg/L**.\\n- In a report involving 4 mothers at two months postpartum: average milk concentrations were **26.4 mcg/L** for sertraline and **29 mcg/L** for norsertraline.\\n- In a report involving the mother of a preterm infant, milk concentrations averaged **201 mcg/L** for sertraline and **358 mcg/L** for norsertraline over three days.\\n- One woman\u2019s milk sertraline concentration averaged **29 mcg/L** at two unspecified sampling times.\\n\\nThese are research measurements, not administered amounts or treatment instructions. The retrieved LactMed extract did not include an infant-level concentration passage; the specimen type and timing for infant-level measurements are therefore missing in this extract. The Drug Levels section was truncated, so additional measurement context may be missing. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\n### Observed infant outcomes\\n\\nLactMed reports:\\n\\n- One **4-month-old infant** had benign neonatal sleep myoclonus and agitation that resolved spontaneously in a case reported in the context of maternal sertraline use.\\n- In a group of **26 infants**, with average age **16.6 weeks** and range **4\u201328 weeks**, the retrieved passage reported no detectable acute adverse reactions to sertraline in breastmilk.\\n- In a study of **14 mothers and their breastfed infants**, whole-blood serotonin levels were measured after 6\u201316 weeks of maternal therapy. Infant levels averaged **227 mcg/L before** and **224 mcg/L after** maternal therapy. The source reported the authors\u2019 conclusion that these findings indicated no effect on platelet serotonin uptake in the infants; this biological finding is not the same as an assessment of all clinical outcomes.\\n\\nThe Effects in Breastfed Infants section was truncated: 24 passages were identified and 19 were omitted from the summary. Some retrieved material did not specify maternal exposure details, extent of breastfeeding, or infant age. These omissions limit interpretation; they do not establish that an outcome was absent. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\n### FAERS report context\\n\\nThe returned FAERS query covered reports matching sertraline generally, not a verified lactation or infant cohort. Its reported terms included nausea (**14,075**), \u201cdrug ineffective\u201d (**13,855**), fatigue (**13,021**), headache (**11,284**), anxiety (**10,530**), diarrhea (**10,499**), dizziness (**9,741**), and depression (**9,612**).\\n\\nThese are reporting volumes, not incidence rates, confirmed clinical outcomes, or proof of causation. The query had no exposure denominator, and the source population was not confirmed; these results cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to sertraline. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22sertraline%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S13](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)\\n\\n### Source and literature limitations\\n\\n- LactMed\u2019s Drug Levels and Effects in Breastfed Infants sections were truncated, so this is not a complete LactMed record. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- The LactMed extract mentions case reports, observational material, and a meta-analysis, but the retrieved record does not establish a complete study count or assign a design to every finding. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- The PubMed search was bounded and not a systematic review. Abstract text was retrieved for **3 of 5** requested records; no abstract text was returned for PMID **38133585** and PMID **32320387**. No records were unreturned or failed abstract lookups. Missing abstracts are retrieval limitations, not evidence that the studies or other research do not exist. Titles alone were not used as outcome evidence. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22sertraline%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json) [S44](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32320387/) [S47](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38133585/)\\n\\nThe selected DailyMed product label was **SERTRALINE HYDROCHLORIDE TABLET [REMEDYREPACK INC.]**, effective November 5, 2026. Its retrieved medicine-taker section lists adult label adverse reactions and warnings including suicidal thoughts and behaviors, serotonin syndrome, increased bleeding risk, mania/hypomania, seizures, hyponatremia, and sexual dysfunction. These are label information for the person taking the medicine, not observed outcomes in breastfed infants. The retrieved label omitted the standalone warnings, warnings-and-precautions, boxed-warning, and drug-interaction sections; missing sections do not establish absence of information. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)\\n\\n### Questions for a clinician or pharmacist\\n\\n1. Which evidence best matches the infant\u2019s age, prematurity status, breastfeeding extent, and health?\\n2. Which findings are milk measurements, and which are observed infant clinical outcomes?\\n3. How should the single case involving agitation and sleep myoclonus be interpreted given the reported timing and the limited case information?\\n4. How should the reported milk-supply observations be interpreted in the context of the lactation history?\\n5. What information is missing because the LactMed sections and some PubMed records are incomplete?\\n6. Are there relevant co-medications or other clinical factors that should be considered?\\n7. What benefits, risks, and follow-up questions should be addressed before making an individualized medication decision?\\n\\nThe MCP-generated continuity-of-care notice states that stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks and should be discussed with the prescribing clinician; this summary does not determine an individualized treatment plan.\\n\\nApplication limits:\\nThese FAERS results cover only the queried report subset. request.question: Give a balanced research summary of sertraline during lactation, with adverse findings and the relevant source context together. Distinguish observed infant outcomes from milk measurements, describe limits in study size or design, and prepare questions for a clinician. No treatment decisions.

## Sertraline during lactation

Sertraline was matched exactly as the single ingredient sertraline, RxNorm ID 36437. [S53](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/36437/properties.json)

### Effects reported in the lactating person

LactMed reports:

- A midwife observed **6 patients who reported decreased milk supply after starting sertraline**; administered amounts were not reported.
- In one of those reports, the mother had taken sertraline since the sixth month of pregnancy, reported increased milk supply during a one-week interruption at four months postpartum, and reported decreased supply after restarting. The source does not establish the exact elapsed time between restarting and the reported decrease.
- LactMed also describes galactorrhea reports in nonpregnant, nonbreastfeeding patients and cites a French pharmacovigilance study in which sertraline was not found to have an increased risk of hyperprolactinemia compared with other drugs.

These are source-reported observations from a limited extract; the retrieved material does not establish a definitive study count. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Measured exposure in milk

The retrieved LactMed record reported the following **milk concentrations**:

- In a pooled analysis of 15 mothers: sertraline averaged **45 mcg/L**, range **7–207 mcg/L**.
- In a study of 26 women with extensive milk and serum sampling over 24 hours: sertraline averaged **129 mcg/L**, range **11–938 mcg/L**; norsertraline averaged **258 mcg/L**, range **20–1498 mcg/L**.
- In a report involving 4 mothers at two months postpartum: average milk concentrations were **26.4 mcg/L** for sertraline and **29 mcg/L** for norsertraline.
- In a report involving the mother of a preterm infant, milk concentrations averaged **201 mcg/L** for sertraline and **358 mcg/L** for norsertraline over three days.
- One woman’s milk sertraline concentration averaged **29 mcg/L** at two unspecified sampling times.

These are research measurements, not administered amounts or treatment instructions. The retrieved LactMed extract did not include an infant-level concentration passage; the specimen type and timing for infant-level measurements are therefore missing in this extract. The Drug Levels section was truncated, so additional measurement context may be missing. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Observed infant outcomes

LactMed reports:

- One **4-month-old infant** had benign neonatal sleep myoclonus and agitation that resolved spontaneously in a case reported in the context of maternal sertraline use.
- In a group of **26 infants**, with average age **16.6 weeks** and range **4–28 weeks**, the retrieved passage reported no detectable acute adverse reactions to sertraline in breastmilk.
- In a study of **14 mothers and their breastfed infants**, whole-blood serotonin levels were measured after 6–16 weeks of maternal therapy. Infant levels averaged **227 mcg/L before** and **224 mcg/L after** maternal therapy. The source reported the authors’ conclusion that these findings indicated no effect on platelet serotonin uptake in the infants; this biological finding is not the same as an assessment of all clinical outcomes.

The Effects in Breastfed Infants section was truncated: 24 passages were identified and 19 were omitted from the summary. Some retrieved material did not specify maternal exposure details, extent of breastfeeding, or infant age. These omissions limit interpretation; they do not establish that an outcome was absent. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### FAERS report context

The returned FAERS query covered reports matching sertraline generally, not a verified lactation or infant cohort. Its reported terms included nausea (**14,075**), “drug ineffective” (**13,855**), fatigue (**13,021**), headache (**11,284**), anxiety (**10,530**), diarrhea (**10,499**), dizziness (**9,741**), and depression (**9,612**).

These are reporting volumes, not incidence rates, confirmed clinical outcomes, or proof of causation. The query had no exposure denominator, and the source population was not confirmed; these results cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to sertraline. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22sertraline%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S13](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

### Source and literature limitations

- LactMed’s Drug Levels and Effects in Breastfed Infants sections were truncated, so this is not a complete LactMed record. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- The LactMed extract mentions case reports, observational material, and a meta-analysis, but the retrieved record does not establish a complete study count or assign a design to every finding. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- The PubMed search was bounded and not a systematic review. Abstract text was retrieved for **3 of 5** requested records; no abstract text was returned for PMID **38133585** and PMID **32320387**. No records were unreturned or failed abstract lookups. Missing abstracts are retrieval limitations, not evidence that the studies or other research do not exist. Titles alone were not used as outcome evidence. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22sertraline%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json) [S44](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32320387/) [S47](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38133585/)

The selected DailyMed product label was **SERTRALINE HYDROCHLORIDE TABLET [REMEDYREPACK INC.]**, effective November 5, 2026. Its retrieved medicine-taker section lists adult label adverse reactions and warnings including suicidal thoughts and behaviors, serotonin syndrome, increased bleeding risk, mania/hypomania, seizures, hyponatremia, and sexual dysfunction. These are label information for the person taking the medicine, not observed outcomes in breastfed infants. The retrieved label omitted the standalone warnings, warnings-and-precautions, boxed-warning, and drug-interaction sections; missing sections do not establish absence of information. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

### Questions for a clinician or pharmacist

1. Which evidence best matches the infant’s age, prematurity status, breastfeeding extent, and health?
2. Which findings are milk measurements, and which are observed infant clinical outcomes?
3. How should the single case involving agitation and sleep myoclonus be interpreted given the reported timing and the limited case information?
4. How should the reported milk-supply observations be interpreted in the context of the lactation history?
5. What information is missing because the LactMed sections and some PubMed records are incomplete?
6. Are there relevant co-medications or other clinical factors that should be considered?
7. What benefits, risks, and follow-up questions should be addressed before making an individualized medication decision?

No treatment decisions.\"}", "response_preview": "{\"answer\": \"## Lamotrigine pregnancy evidence\\n\\nThis evidence brief concerns **lamotrigine** as a single ingredient. It is a bounded evidence summary, not a systematic review; the retrieved PubMed records had abstract text available, but the search was not exhaustive. [S21](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/28439/properties.json) [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22lamotrigine%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Pregnancy%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+pregnan%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+gestation%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)\\n\\n### Maternal effects and underlying disease\\n\\nThe selected DailyMed label states that **epilepsy, with or without antiseizure-medication exposure, has been associated with** preeclampsia, preterm labor, antepartum and postpartum hemorrhage, placental abruption, poor fetal growth, prematurity, fetal death, and maternal mortality. It also states that maternal or fetal injury may be greatest with untreated or poorly controlled convulsive seizures. These are label statements about underlying disease and pregnancy context, not findings that lamotrigine caused each outcome. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)\\n\\nThe label also states that physiological changes during pregnancy may affect lamotrigine concentrations and therapeutic effect, with reports of decreased concentrations during pregnancy and restoration of pre-pregnancy concentrations after delivery. The retrieved extract does not provide a validated individualized pharmacokinetic plan. request.question: Summarize lamotrigine pregnancy evidence for a research discussion, retaining label context about underlying disease alongside adverse findings. Keep maternal effects, exposure and infant outcomes separate, with limitations and questions for the clinician. No treatment decisions.

response.answer:
## Lamotrigine pregnancy evidence

This evidence brief concerns **lamotrigine** as a single ingredient. It is a bounded evidence summary, not a systematic review; the retrieved PubMed records had abstract text available, but the search was not exhaustive. [S21](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/28439/properties.json) [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22lamotrigine%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Pregnancy%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+pregnan%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+gestation%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)

### Maternal effects and underlying disease

The selected DailyMed label states that **epilepsy, with or without antiseizure-medication exposure, has been associated with** preeclampsia, preterm labor, antepartum and postpartum hemorrhage, placental abruption, poor fetal growth, prematurity, fetal death, and maternal mortality. It also states that maternal or fetal injury may be greatest with untreated or poorly controlled convulsive seizures. These are label statements about underlying disease and pregnancy context, not findings that lamotrigine caused each outcome. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The label also states that physiological changes during pregnancy may affect lamotrigine concentrations and therapeutic effect, with reports of decreased concentrations during pregnancy and restoration of pre-pregnancy concentrations after delivery. The retrieved extract does not provide a validated individualized pharmacokinetic plan. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

### Maternal pharmacokinetics

The retrieved label passages describe changes in lamotrigine concentrations during pregnancy, but no numeric maternal concentration data were returned in this summary. A review abstract describes pregnancy-related changes in antiseizure-medication levels, but the retrieved passage does not establish a lamotrigine-specific study population or design. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4) [S14](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32768086/)

### Fetal or infant exposure

No verified numeric **fetal** lamotrigine concentration was retrieved.

A mixed pregnancy/lactation study included **60 mothers** and examined medication concentrations in serum and breastmilk at different time points, with child development assessed during the first 12 months. Its abstract reported a high concentration-by-dose ratio in breastmilk for lamotrigine, but the retrieved extract supplied no lamotrigine-specific concentration value, no fetal concentration, and no infant specimen result. The population was mixed—pregnancy, lactation, neonates, and children—so it should not be generalized to fetal exposure during pregnancy. [S17](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)

The label reports animal findings in pregnant rats involving decreased fetal folate concentrations. This is animal evidence, not measured human fetal exposure. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

### Observed fetal or infant outcomes

The selected label reports the following registry findings:

- **International Lamotrigine Pregnancy Registry:** major congenital malformations in **2.2%** of **1,558** infants exposed to lamotrigine monotherapy during the first trimester; reported 95% CI, **1.6%–3.1%**.
- **NAAED Pregnancy Registry:** major congenital malformations among **2.0%** of **1,562** infants exposed to lamotrigine monotherapy during the first trimester.
- In another NAAED analysis, isolated oral clefts were reported at **3.2 per 1,000** among **2,200** infants exposed early in pregnancy; the label describes this as a threefold increase versus unexposed healthy controls.

The label states that differences in outcome definitions, ascertainment methods, and comparator groups limit the conclusions. It also states that the available data did not suggest increased risk of the listed outcomes with lamotrigine monotherapy exposure; this is a source statement with the stated limitations, not an overall safety conclusion. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The label says that meta-analyses evaluated fetal death, stillbirth, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth, and neurodevelopmental delay, but the retrieved extract does not provide lamotrigine-specific estimates for those outcomes. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

### FAERS report-only context

For the queried pregnancy-exposure report subset, FAERS returned:

| Reported term | Reports |
|---|---:|
| Foetal exposure during pregnancy | 3,527 |
| Atrial septal defect | 357 |
| Congenital anomaly | 327 |
| Premature baby | 257 |
| Ventricular septal defect | 205 |
| Patent ductus arteriosus | 153 |
| Spina bifida | 143 |
| Hypospadias | 135 |

These counts are reporting volume, not incidence, confirmed clinical outcomes, or proof of causation. The query had no exposure denominator and covered only the matched report subset; the source population was not confirmed for every report and cannot be generalized to all infants or all exposed people. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22lamotrigine%22+AND+patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt%3A%22foetal+exposure+during+pregnancy%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S12](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

### Label and evidence limitations

The selected DailyMed record was one lamotrigine product label, not all formulations. Its pregnancy section was marked truncated, and the returned extraction did not include the label’s adult adverse-reaction, warnings, warnings-and-precautions, boxed-warning, or drug-interaction sections. Missing sections are extraction limitations, not evidence that those sections contain no information. DailyMed also states that in-use labeling can differ from the latest FDA-approved labeling. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The retrieved brief did not identify a curated federal pregnancy counterpart to LactMed; pregnancy evidence therefore came from product labeling and literature in this lookup, with non-exhaustive coverage. [S24](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/labeling/questions-and-answers-pregnancy-and-lactation-labeling-rule) [S25](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501922/)

### Questions for the clinician

- How closely do the registry populations match the relevant pregnancy timing, indication, seizure history, and monotherapy or polytherapy context?
- Which findings are registry observations, which are label summaries of meta-analyses, and which are spontaneous reports?
- What lamotrigine-specific evidence is available for neurodevelopment, preterm birth, fetal growth, stillbirth, and fetal death?
- How should the underlying condition and the label’s seizure-related context be incorporated into interpretation?
- Which uncertainties arise from the truncated pregnancy section and missing adult warning sections?

The MCP-generated continuity-of-care notice states that stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks and should be discussed with the prescribing clinician. This summary does not determine an individual benefit–risk balance.

Application limits:
These FAERS results cover only the queried report subset. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to the medicine, and cannot establish incidence or causation.
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.
Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.
Structured evidence rows (retrieval inventory)
| Evidence axis | Extracted findings | Context-only passages | Gap statements |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Effect on the pregnant or lactating person | 1 extracted candidate passages; source interpretation requires review. | 0 | 1 |
| Measured transfer or exposure to fetus or infant | 3 extracted candidate passages; source interpretation requires review. | 2 | 1 |
| Observed outcomes in fetus or infant | 6 extracted candidate passages; source interpretation requires review. | 5 | 1 |
These are counts of extracted passages, not studies or proven effects. Context-only passages and gap statements are counted separately. Empty rows do not establish absence of evidence elsewhere or safety. This inventory does not replace the cited findings or validate applicability.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

### Fetal or infant exposure

No verified numeric **fetal** lamotrigine concentration was retrieved.

A mixed pregnancy/lactation study included **60 mothers** and examined medication concentrations in serum and breastmilk at different time points, with child development assessed during the first 12 months. Its abstract reported a high concentration-by-dose ratio in breastmilk for lamotrigine, but the retrieved extract supplied no lamotrigine-specific concentration value, no fetal concentration, and no infant specimen result. The population was mixed—pregnancy, lactation, neonates, and children—so it should not be generalized to fetal exposure during pregnancy. [S17](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)

The label reports animal findings in pregnant rats involving decreased fetal folate concentrations. This is animal evidence, not measured human fetal exposure. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

### Observed fetal or infant outcomes

The selected label reports the following registry findings:

- **International Lamotrigine Pregnancy Registry:** major congenital malformations in **2.2%** of **1,558** infants exposed to lamotrigine monotherapy during the first trimester; reported 95% CI, **1.6%–3.1%**.
- **NAAED Pregnancy Registry:** major congenital malformations among **2.0%** of **1,562** infants exposed to lamotrigine monotherapy during the first trimester.
- In another NAAED analysis, isolated oral clefts were reported at **3.2 per 1,000** among **2,200** infants exposed early in pregnancy; the label describes this as a threefold increase versus unexposed healthy controls.

The label states that differences in outcome definitions, ascertainment methods, and comparator groups limit the conclusions. It also states that the available data did not suggest increased risk of the listed outcomes with lamotrigine monotherapy exposure; this is a source statement with the stated limitations, not an overall safety conclusion. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The label says that meta-analyses evaluated fetal death, stillbirth, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth, and neurodevelopmental delay, but the retrieved extract does not provide lamotrigine-specific estimates for those outcomes. ### Label and evidence limitations

The selected DailyMed record was one lamotrigine product label, not all formulations. Its pregnancy section was marked truncated, and the returned extraction did not include the label’s adult adverse-reaction, warnings, warnings-and-precautions, boxed-warning, or drug-interaction sections. Missing sections are extraction limitations, not evidence that those sections contain no information. DailyMed also states that in-use labeling can differ from the latest FDA-approved labeling. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The retrieved brief did not identify a curated federal pregnancy counterpart to LactMed; pregnancy evidence therefore came from product labeling and literature in this lookup, with non-exhaustive coverage. [S24](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/labeling/questions-and-answers-pregnancy-and-lactation-labeling-rule) [S25](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501922/)

### Questions for the clinician

- How closely do the registry populations match the relevant pregnancy timing, indication, seizure history, and monotherapy or polytherapy context?
- Which findings are registry observations, which are label summaries of meta-analyses, and which are spontaneous reports?
- What lamotrigine-specific evidence is available for neurodevelopment, preterm birth, fetal growth, stillbirth, and fetal death?
- How should the underlying condition and the label’s seizure-related context be incorporated into interpretation?
- Which uncertainties arise from the truncated pregnancy section and missing adult warning sections?
